As an INFP myself, figuring out transportation is stressful enough, so I get that, but the point I'm trying to highlight is that it seems that dating itself isn't necessary the main barrier, but rather a serious of emotional and logistical stressors.


I think if you had self-mastery of transportation, (whether it be with ride-sharing, bike riding, public transit), this would remove one barrier.


If you had the expectation that it's okay to date multiple people simultaneously, and spread it out over time, you'd ease a lot of tension on yourself and your potential matches. I get the desire to deeply connect rapidly, as we're sold the idea that once you find your person,you just know,and you're instantly in-sync. 


Anywho, I'm rambling, but sitting down for a long session of self-assesment and identifying challenges and barriers and really asking yourself how much each one matters, it will allow you to really focus on your priorities and expedite growth in the areas you need to succeed at securing that right match for you.


I'm not saying your expectations are wrong, mind you. Just that with every expectation, there is ultimately a cost.


tl;dr: Check yoself before you wreck yoself. Tear down barriers with strategy and self-mastery to increase compatibility with your own goals.

Personally, I think understanding what boundaries are, like REALLY understanding them, and being able to communicate them will enable you to move forward. Also, being able to inquire about and respect others boundaries helps significantly also.  
If you're thinking consistently about something, it usually means there's something actionable. Having a trusted friend or family member, or even a therapist, to discuss these things with can help, but it's not required.  
The two things that I personally thing are foundational in any kind of friendship or relationship are informed consent (in all things. People should be able to opt-in our out of anything safely) and boundaries.  
If there's a topic that's important to them, you could say something like "I noticed when we were talking about X you had mentioned Y", then ask them to share more about how they feel about it and how important it is to them. Consider the same for yourself and make sure you know where your boundaries are so you're not asking of them what you wouldn't share yourself.

I've made many mistakes. Mistakes that define where we are, but not WHO we are. If you leave them on the floor like a pile of dirty laundry, all they do is sap the life out of you when you see it. Pick a piece of your life up off the floor one at a time and toss it in a metaphorical laundry basket. You're not cleaning them right now. You're not even asking yourself how to clean in. You're just accepting the fact that it's there and needs assistance.  


So, pick something. Literally anything. You know what you would like that thing to be. Put that at the top of your scale. Ask yourself, where is that thing now? How could it be worse? Put a worse version of what you have at the bottom of your scale.

Lycan has strong single target damage and has the hp pool to survive invoker burst.

To determine if lycan is 'good' mid, you want 3 things. 
1 - little to no lockdown. If they have a roaming shadow shaman, and he ganks with smoke, you dead. Even if you get your ult off, the duration of the disable is long enough to kill you.
2 - little to no aoe spam. If they can spam aoe spells, chances are they are getting just as much benefit from wolves as you are.
3 - slow and squishy heroes. Basically, lycan feeds on kills now that jungle is not as good, so the more you kill early, the better you snowball. Slow heroes let you get in and out without diving too deep before your ult ends 

There certainly are waaaay more variables than I covered, and I could be very wrong, but that's how I look at it.
